title: A piezoelectric energy harvester for broadband rotational excitation using buckled beam

sections.heading: A piezoelectric energy harvester for broadband rotational excitation using buckled beam
sections.text:

sections.heading: A piezoelectric energy harvester for broadband rotational excitation using buckled beam
sections.text:
Zhengqiu Xie,1 C. A. Kitio Kwuimy,3 Zhiguo Wang,1 and Wenbin Huang1,2,a

1The State Key Lab of Mechanical Transmissions, Chongqing University,   
Chongqing 400044, China   
2Anhui Province Laboratory of Electrical Economize and Safety, Anhui University,   
Hefei 230601, China   
3Department of Engineering Education, College of Engineering and Applied Science,   
University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH 45220, USA

(Received 3 December 2017; accepted 11 January 2018; published online 22 January 2018)

This paper proposes a rotational energy harvester using a piezoelectric bistable buckled beam to harvest low-speed rotational energy. The proposed harvester consists of a piezoelectric buckled beam with a center magnet, and a rotary magnet pair with opposite magnetic poles mounted on a revolving host. The magnetic plucking is used to harvest the angular kinetic energy of the host. The nonlinear snap-through mechanism is utilized to improve the vibration displacement and output voltage of the piezoelectric layer over a wide rotation frequency range. Theoretical simulation and experimental results show that the proposed energy harvester can yield a stable average output power ranging between $6 . 9 1 \substack { - 4 8 . 0 1 \ \mu \mathrm { W } }$ over a rotation frequency range of $1 { - } 1 4 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ across a resistance load of $1 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Furthermore, dual attraction magnets were employed to overcome the suppression phenomenon at higher frequencies, which yields a broadband and flat frequency response over $6 { \cdot } 1 4 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ with the output power reaching 42.19- $6 5 . 4 4 \mu \mathrm { W } ,$ demonstrating the great potential of the bistable buckled beam for wideband rotation motion energy harvesting. $©$ 2018 Author(s). sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
With the developing of wearable electronics and wireless communication, energy harvesting from mechanical vibration in ambient environmental has been gaining increasing attention in the past two decades.1–4 The main transduction mechanisms can be divided in three groups: electromagnetic,5 electrostatic,6 and piezoelectric.7–9 Among these transduction mechanisms, the piezoelectric transduction has attracted the most interest due to its high power density and simple structure. 10

Most researchers focus on the scavenging of linear vibration energy which is ubiquitous in the ambient environment.11–14 In contrast, rotational energy has been less studied and used as the power source. Nevertheless, energy harvester to collect energy from rotary motion can be very useful for many practical applications, such as the condition monitoring of rotating machine,15 tire pressure monitoring,16 and wind energy harvesting.17 Kan et al.18 developed a piezo-disk energy harvester excited by rotary magnets. Zhang et al.19 investigated the energy harvesting for the practical tire application using a bistable cantilever structure. Pozzi20 developed a compact and low-profile energy harvester to harvest the kinetic energy of knee-joint, where the non-contact magnetic plucking mechanism was used to realize the frequency up-conversion. Energy harvesting systems with piezoelectric cantilever and tip mass mounted on a rotating shaft have been investigated.15,21 Fu and Yeatman22 developed a piezoelectric turbine using the magnetic plucking between the piezoelectric beam and the passing rotor. More recently, they23 developed a low-speed rotational energy harvesting system consisting of a piezoelectric cantilever with a tip mass and a rotating magnet on a revolving host. Zou et al.24 presented a rotational energy harvesting system with two inverted piezoelectric cantilevers which are magnetically coupled with each other.

From the literature, it can be found that piezoelectric cantilever is the main structure employed for rotational energy harvesting due to the simple configuration. To widen the frequency bandwidth and enhance the power output, nonlinear magnetic mechanism has been widely used to construct a bistable system. Stanton et al.25 proposed a bistable inertial oscillator comprised of a piezoelectric cantilever beam and magnets, and theoretically and experimentally demonstrated its enhanced energy harvesting performance. Erturk and Inman26 investigated the high-energy orbits of a proposed non-resonant piezomagnetoelastic energy harvester over a broad excitation frequency range. Zhou et al.27 adjusted the angular orientation of the rotatable external magnets to enhanced the operational frequency bandwidth of the magnetically coupled nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvester.

On the other side, as a compact bistable system with a large snap through distance, buckled beam has been widely studied for linear vibration energy harvesting.28–32 Zhang et al.33 developed a piezoelectric wind energy harvester using a buckled beam to achieve large amplitude vibrations. The experimental results show that buckled beam can increase the root-mean-square (RMS) voltage by nearly five times at $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m / s }$ wind speed compared with conventional cantilever beam harvester. Jiang et al.34 proposed a multi-step energy harvester by utilizing a buckled beam driven by magnetic excitation, and demonstrated that the buckled beam is capable of resonating under low frequency oscillations. Liu et al.35 studied a compact nonlinear bistable energy harvester with wide bandwidth using double buckled beams. Meanwhile, Harne and $\mathrm { W a n g ^ { 3 6 } }$ showed that the axial compression and compliant suspensions could dramatically improve the performance of the buckled beam energy harvesting system.

From the above literature review, it can be found that buckled beams could enhance the frequency bandwidth and output power of the energy harvester. However, buckled piezoelectric beam has not been investigated for rotational energy harvesting. In this paper, we proposed a buckled piezoelectric beam for low-speed rotational energy harvesting. The rotation of magnets array could induce a periodically switching magnetic force upon the buckled piezoelectric beam, leading to the snapthrough motion of the buckled beam and improve the operational frequency bandwidth with high output power. Theoretical analysis model to simulate the electro-magneto-mechanical coupling was presented. Energy harvesters with single and dual attraction magnets were compared over a wide frequency range. Both the theoretical simulation and experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the harvester with dual attraction magnets.

sections.heading: II. DESIGN AND MODELING
sections.text:
The schematic of the rotational energy harvester using buckled piezoelectric beam is shown in Fig. 1(a). It consists of a buckled beam with the magnet A attached at the center and a piezoelectric patch attached near the bottom end of the buckled beam. Two magnets (B and C) with opposite magnetization directions are stuck to the revolving host with a $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ phase difference. Fig. 1(b) shows that with the stepper motor rotating, the magnetic force between revolving magnets and the center magnets would cause the buckled beam to snap through between two stable positions.

sections.heading: III. PROTOTYPE AND EXPERIMENTS
sections.text:
The experiment set-up is shown in Fig. 3. A stepper motor (SS1704A20A-01, Samsr motor) with the step angle of $1 . 8 ^ { \circ }$ is placed near the buckled beam, and a revolving disk is installed on the motor’s shaft. Two magnets are glued on the disk, and the rotational radius of rotary magnets is $2 4 \mathrm { m m }$ . The buckled beam is made of brass, and the piezoelectric patch is composed of lead zirconate titanate (PZT-5H). The dimension of the buckled beam is $1 7 5 { \times } 1 2 { \times } 0 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ . The capacitance of the PZT patch with the dimension of $2 2 { \times } 8 { \times } 0 . 2 4 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ is measured to be $2 0 ~ \mathrm { n F }$ using a LCR meter (UCE UC2831). The separation between two stable positions of the buckled beam is $6 \mathrm { m m }$ and $d _ { x 0 } ^ { N }$ is $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ . The size of each magnet is $1 0 { \times } 1 0 { \times } 1 0 \ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ . The magnetization of magnets is $1 . 2 6 \mathrm { T } ,$ and the mass of each magnet is $7 . 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ . A digital oscilloscope (TDS 2024C, Tektronix) was used to collect data of the generated voltage.

The harvester is tested under different excitation frequencies ( $1 { - } 1 4 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ with the step size of $1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ ). To investigate the influences of attractive force and repelling force to the performance of the energy harvester, three prototypes with different numbers of attraction or repulsion magnets were studied, including the single attraction-single repulsion (SASR), dual attraction-single repulsion (DASR) and dual attraction-dual repulsion (DADR), respectively. The average output power can be expressed as

$$
P = ( V _ { r m s } ) ^ { 2 } / R
$$

where $V _ { r m s }$ is the root-mean-square of the output voltage.

FIG. 3. Prototypes of the energy harvester: (a) single attraction magnet and single repulsion magnet, (b) dual attraction magnets and single repulsion magnet, (c) dual attraction magnets and dual repulsion magnets.

sections.heading: IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Fig. 4 shows the experimental output voltage of the harvester with a single attraction magnet and a single repulsion magnet under the rotation excitation frequency of $1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ across a resistive load of 1 MΩ. The theoretical simulation results are also plotted for comparison. It can be observed that the theoretical simulation results are in good agreement with the experimental results. Simultaneously, the experimental results show that the buckled beam could snap twice in one period. This is due to the parallel layout of the rotary magnets on the disk. Assuming the magnet A to reside around the stable position close to the disk originally, the approaching magnet B could generate a repelling force to push the magnet A to snap to another stable position at the far end. The magnet A will vibrate around the stable position and gradually damp out as the magnet B gets away from it. Later, the attractive force induced by the magnet C gradually increases as it approaches to the magnet A. The force will become large enough to drag the magnet A to snap to the stable position near to the disk. It can be found that the amplitude of the output voltage is about $7 . 2 2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ for each snap-though phenomenon occurrence.

Fig. 5 illustrates the RMS voltage of the simulations and experiments of the SASR, DASR and DADR over $1 { - } 1 4 \mathrm { H z }$ rotation frequency range across a resistive load of $1 \ : \mathbf { M } \Omega$ . It can be observed that the simulation results are in good accordance with the experimental results. The RMS voltages of three prototypes are all found to gradually increase with the rotation frequency below $7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . This is because that the snap through phenomenon occurs more frequently at higher rotation speed, resulting into a larger RMS voltage output. The average power is shown in Fig. 6 with a load resistance of $1 1 0 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . The peak average power of the SASR, DASR and DADR are $4 8 . 0 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } _ { : }$ , $6 5 . 4 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ and $6 1 . 1 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at the rotation frequency of $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively. When the rotation frequency exceeds $7 \mathrm { H z }$ , the output of SASR decreases and reaches the minimum at around $1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . However, the DASR and DADR experience a relative flat frequency response above $6 \mathrm { H z }$ with comparable energy outputs which are $27 \%$ higher than that of the SASR.

![](images/cfdfd80682b63d2b69e3865aa3dcb7723945b0b64594d8331d4686e8c042da16.jpg)  
FIG. 4. The output voltage of the harvester across a resistive load of 1MΩ at the rotation frequency of $1 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ .

![](images/93432a18c42d1d35a3e681faecef49defc2c24e188eca05ea7f7aa2cecf19d10.jpg)  
FIG. 5. RMS voltage with a load resistance of $1 \ : \mathrm { M } \Omega$ at different rotation frequencies.

![](images/ca20fff84d8c62bad8e631252f7e2dd04a70232513c3fa696f8adf7a8246bee7.jpg)  
FIG. 6. Average power with a load resistance of $1 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ under different rotation frequencies.

To exploit the reason for the decrease of SASR’s output after $7 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , the output open-circuit voltage waveforms of SASR and DASR under the rotational excitation frequencies of $7 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ are plotted in Fig. 7. At $7 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , SASR and DASR show similar output voltage with large amplitude, corresponding to a persistent snap through phenomenon. However, the output voltage of SASR becomes much smaller at $1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ in most time. This indicates that the attractive force is always not enough to drag the buckled beam to the stable position at the near end, leaving the beam vibrating around the stable position at the far side and generating a low output voltage. In contrast, the output voltage of the DASR maintains a high level at $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ with continuous snap through occurrences. On the other side, the comparable performances of DASR and DADR demonstrate that the repulsive force is enough to trigger the snap-through phenomenon for DASR, and the further increase of it is unable to enlarge the output power. This is mainly attributed the different spatial distributions of the attractive force and repulsive force as the buckled beam vibrates. The repulsive force dominates when the buckled beam reaches the stable position at the near end, while the attractive force is supposed to drag the buckled beam from the stable position at the far end. Therefore, due to the shorter distance between the repulsive magnet to the magnet A, the repulsive force is much larger than the attractive force and could sustain the snap-through occurrence at high rotation speeds.

![](images/36312e0065dd61d7f0035a859e795162e67bcb63d112b2efd5379e1195b6e972.jpg)  
FIG. 7. Output voltages of (a) SASR and (b) DASR at the rotational excitation frequencies of $7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ .

sections.heading: V. CONCLUSION
sections.text: In conclusion, a piezoelectric buckled beam was proposed to harvest energy from low-speed broadband rotational motion. The average power of SASR could reach $6 . 9 1 \mathrm { - } 4 8 . 0 1 \mu \mathrm { W }$ with a $1 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ load resistance under the rotation excitation frequency range of $1 { - } 1 4 \mathrm { H z }$ . A good agreement between the experimental observations and theoretical simulation was obtained. In order to overcome the suppression phenomenon of SASR at higher frequencies, DASR with larger attractive force were developed and investigated. It was found that the DASR could yield a $27 \%$ enhancement of the average power output compared with that of the SASR. Moreover, a very broadband and flat frequency response between $6 { \sim } 1 4 \mathrm { H z }$ can be obtained by DASR, with the output power about $4 2 . 1 9 \mathrm { - } 6 5 . 4 4 \mu \mathrm { W }$ . It was also observed that the output performance of the DADR is no better than the DASR. These findings demonstrate the great potential of DASR for broadband rotation motion energy harvesting applications including the condition monitoring of rotating machinery, environmental monitoring and tire condition monitoring, etc.
